title: Produce a transplantable, fully engineered living human heart

concept.text: The innovation would be a manufactured, living human heart that could be transplanted to replace a failing heart and sustain the recipient’s circulation. It would require an integrated organ: chambers that fill and pump, valves that direct blood flow, coronary vessels that nourish the tissue, coordinated electrical activation, and sufficiently mature muscle to perform sustained physiological work. These are engineering requirements for the proposed capability, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

Engineered myocardial tissue provides a foundation for this goal. Jebran and colleagues demonstrated implantation of engineered heart muscle onto existing hearts, including evidence of retained graft tissue in a human recipient. The proposed advance extends beyond adding muscle to a functioning organ: the manufactured heart would itself have to provide the coordinated vascular, electrical and mechanical functions needed for replacement.

significance.text: Conditional on durable function, safe transplantation and reproducible manufacture, this capability would create a source of replacement human hearts independent of donated whole hearts. Its revolutionary consequence would be the ability to manufacture an integrated living replacement organ. This is a capability-based inference; the supplied tissue-engineering results do not establish that such an organ can yet be produced.

A scalable platform could make organ availability more predictable and expand access to replacement therapy. Those downstream possibilities depend on production capacity, affordability, delivery logistics and clinical suitability. Manufacturing a working heart would therefore not, by itself, establish that donor scarcity had been eliminated or that treatment was broadly accessible.

Patient-matched cells might reduce immune incompatibility, but freedom from immunosuppression would require direct demonstration. In the supplied Jebran study, withdrawal of immunosuppression after three months led to rejection of allograft cardiomyocytes, and immune responses were also documented in a macaque autograft. These observations make immune management a substantive concern, while neither proving that every patient-matched approach would require immunosuppression nor demonstrating that matching reliably avoids it.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reproducible integration at whole-organ scale. A proposed engineered heart would need appropriate anatomy and material properties so that its chambers, valves, vessels and muscle work together under physiological loading. Producing living cardiac tissue or observing contraction would not establish that the construct could fill, eject blood, maintain directional flow and support the recipient’s circulation. The supplied record does not establish this integrated capability.

Vascularization is a central scaling barrier. The Jebran study identifies functional vascularization as necessary for sustained myocardial remuscularization and documents vascularized grafts. Extending this to a replacement organ would require a coronary circulation capable of supporting the entire living construct. Graft vascularization establishes an enabling step, not adequate perfusion of a manufactured whole heart.

Muscle maturation, coordinated activation and immune compatibility also remain critical requirements. The supplied review identifies relative cardiomyocyte immaturity and immune-management challenges in the Jebran grafts. For whole-organ replacement, engineering would additionally need to establish sufficient mechanical performance and reliable electrical coordination without dangerous rhythm disturbances. The source grounds these concerns at tissue scale; it does not establish the state of every possible whole-organ approach.

A further proposed engineering requirement is reliable manufacture and delivery: repeated production of organs with consistent anatomy, viable tissue and verified function, followed by preservation and transplantation without losing those properties. Durability over years must be demonstrated separately from initial viability or short-term pumping. These requirements extend the concept beyond the capabilities verified in the supplied record.

current_state.text: Jebran and colleagues reported engineered heart muscle patches implanted on existing hearts, with follow-up extending to six months in macaques. The supplied review describes vascularized myocardial grafts and evidence relevant to remuscularization, alongside maturation and immune-management limitations. These are demonstrations of implanted tissue for heart repair; they do not demonstrate manufacture or transplantation of a complete engineered heart.

The human evidence described in that review concerns one BioVAT-HF participant whose existing heart received epicardial engineered muscle grafts. Approximately three months after implantation, the patient underwent donor-heart transplantation, allowing examination of the removed heart and confirmation of retained human graft tissue. This establishes graft retention and remuscularization evidence in a single case. It does not establish controlled clinical efficacy, years of performance, or life support by an engineered replacement organ.

The reviewed supplement includes a BioVAT-HF clinical protocol synopsis addressing the safety and efficacy of engineered human myocardium in patients with terminal heart failure. It identifies immune rejection, arrhythmia and mechanical-function assessments as relevant concerns. A protocol synopsis establishes the intended evaluation framework, not completed outcomes, and the reviewed material does not represent the entire underlying clinical protocol.

The supplied research identifies a Min and colleagues paper about perfusable engineered human cardiac tissues and gives a publication date of 22 March 2024. However, the retained PubMed artifact available to the reviewer contained only a cookie-access message. Its abstract, article identity and reported perfusable-tissue findings could not be verified from that artifact. The earlier description of an abstract-based assessment must therefore be withdrawn. This access failure leaves the asserted result unverified within this record; it is not evidence that the result is false.

No complete human-sized engineered replacement heart was established by the evidence assessed in the supplied review. That conclusion is bounded by the reviewed sources and cannot establish field-wide absence. In particular, the freshness record was empty, so the review could not establish the field’s status through 1 November 2026. The supplied review also does not provide a verified publication date for the Jebran report; its six-month animal and approximately three-month human observation periods should not be confused with years of demonstrated durability.

The Jebran findings summarized here come from the supplied review of an untruncated article HTML record and an untruncated supplement containing the clinical synopsis. The main-paper PDF extraction was truncated, but the central patch-versus-organ distinction was explicit in the article text and captions. Figure images were not inspected in that review, so this account does not claim independent visual confirmation of them.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: manufacture complete living human hearts repeatedly, with documented chamber and valve function, coronary perfusion, coordinated electrical activation and mechanical performance under defined physiological conditions. Acceptance criteria should specify pressures, flows, loading conditions, rhythm stability and tissue viability before testing. The supplied sources establish neither numerical whole-organ thresholds nor a consensus completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatedly manufactured living hearts function under predefined physiological conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed translational demonstration: show that the engineered organ can provide durable, life-supporting replacement function in appropriate preclinical models, followed by controlled human evaluation with follow-up over years. Such studies should distinguish the organ’s contribution from support supplied by other devices or residual native-heart function, and should measure survival, functional performance, rejection and clinically important complications. Comparators, follow-up periods and acceptable risks would need explicit justification.
completion_criteria.label: Life-supporting replacement demonstrated preclinically and through years-long human evaluation

completion_criteria.text: The graft programme provides a concrete basis for including immune rejection, arrhythmias and mechanical function in safety and efficacy assessment. For the proposed whole organ, evaluation must also establish the actual immunosuppression requirement rather than assuming tolerance from cell matching. The BioVAT-HF synopsis supports the relevance of these endpoints, but does not prescribe a whole-organ replacement standard.
completion_criteria.label: Whole-organ evaluation establishes safety, efficacy and actual immunosuppression requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: demonstrate consistent results across manufacturing batches and independent teams, define eligible recipients and failure conditions, and validate preservation, transport and surgical delivery. A claim of broad availability would additionally require evidence on capacity, cost and access. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within tested conditions, not universal reliability across all patients or circumstances.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible manufacturing and validated delivery with defined clinical boundaries

related_concepts.text: CAR-01, “Regenerate a severely damaged adult human heart,” has the closest technical overlap: both involve living muscle, maturation, vascularization, integration and manufacturing. The distinction is the therapeutic unit. Repair adds or restores function within an existing heart; CAR-07 requires a complete replacement organ. The Jebran graft evidence informs the repair-to-replacement boundary, but does not independently validate the full CAR-01 concept.

Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CAR-03, “A durable, broadly affordable total artificial heart,” and CAR-04, “A dependable supply of transplantable animal hearts,” share the goal of replacing a failing heart. They pursue distinct routes: a mechanical device, an animal-derived organ, and a manufactured living human organ, respectively. Evidence for one route does not establish durability, affordability or immune compatibility for another.

Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CAR-05 addresses inherited disease by correction within the beating heart, while CAR-08 and CAR-11 address heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. These target disease mechanisms or physiological burdens rather than manufacture of a replacement organ. Whole-heart replacement would not automatically correct inherited disease in other tissues or resolve disease in the pulmonary circulation.

Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CAR-06 and CAR-09 concern prevention of sudden cardiac death and durable treatment of atrial fibrillation. They overlap with CAR-07 through electrical stability and rhythm safety, but have different endpoints. A replacement heart would need reliable electrical function without thereby demonstrating broad prediction of sudden death or a general cure for atrial fibrillation.

Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CAR-02 and CAR-12 address systemic atherosclerosis and actionable coronary plaque risk; CAR-10 targets established calcific aortic stenosis without valve replacement; CAR-13 seeks prevention of cardiac injury from cancer treatment while preserving cancer control. These remain distinct prevention or disease-reversal goals. Manufacturing coronary vessels and valves would not establish systemic atherosclerosis reversal, plaque-risk detection, reversal of disease in an existing valve, or protection during cancer treatment.

unresolved_issues: The Min paper’s identity, abstract and findings remain unverified within the retained review artifact; its supplied publication date is bibliographic information from the research input.
The empty freshness record leaves field-wide status through 1 November 2026 unresolved. The supplied evidence cannot establish whether other work demonstrated a complete engineered human heart.
A verified publication date for the Jebran report is not supplied in the review.
Whole-organ physiological thresholds, manufacturing tolerances, replication requirements, clinical comparators and justified follow-up durations remain to be defined.
The extent to which patient-matched engineered organs would reduce rejection or immunosuppression requirements remains unknown.
Durable whole-organ performance, scalable production, affordability and practical delivery are not demonstrated by the supplied tissue-graft evidence.

brief.title: Living replacement hearts made to order
possible: People with failing hearts could receive a manufactured living heart instead of waiting for a donated organ. It would replace their heart and sustain blood flow through their body.
The replacement would have chambers that fill and pump, valves that keep blood moving in the right direction, vessels that feed the muscle, and electrical signals that coordinate each beat.
why: Manufacturing replacement hearts would create a supply independent of whole-heart donations. Predictable production could help more patients receive replacement treatment.

sources.showed: Engineered muscle patches survived on macaque hearts and improved measures of pumping in animals with heart failure. Examination of a treated patient's heart confirmed added muscle tissue.
sources.quote: Our clinical data confirmed remuscularization by EHM implantation in a patient with advanced heart failure.
sources.cited_for: Living muscle grown outside the body can survive after implantation and add muscle to an existing heart.
sources.not_established: The patches did not replace a heart or demonstrate that a manufactured organ could sustain someone's circulation.

sources.showed: They built a system that flows fluid through a culture environment containing the material surrounding heart cells. It improved the structure and functional maturity of engineered human heart tissue.
sources.quote: The integrated culture platform of a microfluidic chip and a three-dimensional heart extracellular matrix enhances human cardiac tissue development and their structural and functional maturation.
sources.cited_for: A flowing culture system can improve the development of engineered human heart tissue.
sources.not_established: The work did not demonstrate a complete replacement heart or a blood supply capable of nourishing an entire manufactured organ.

shown: Jebran and colleagues kept implanted muscle patches alive on macaque hearts for up to six months. The patches developed a working blood supply, and animals with heart failure showed evidence of improved pumping.

In a single patient, muscle patches remained on the existing heart until it was removed during a donor-heart transplant. This demonstrated tissue survival, but did not establish lasting clinical benefit or replacement-heart function.
missing: A complete living heart has yet to demonstrate coordinated filling, pumping and reliable blood flow under the body's normal demands.
An internal blood supply must nourish the entire organ, while mature muscle maintains strong contractions and a stable rhythm.
Replacement hearts must sustain recipients for years with acceptable rejection risks and other complications.
Repeated manufacture, preservation, transport and transplantation must consistently retain the organ's function.

milestones.label: Repeatedly manufactured hearts work under defined conditions
milestones.explanation: Repeatedly made hearts would have to pass predefined tests of chambers, valves, blood supply, rhythm and pumping under realistic loads. This would establish integrated organ function.

milestones.label: Replacement hearts sustain life through years of human evaluation
milestones.explanation: Animal studies followed by controlled human evaluation over years would have to establish life-supporting replacement function separately from devices or the native heart. This would establish durable replacement.

milestones.label: Whole hearts demonstrate safety, benefit and immune treatment needs
milestones.explanation: Whole-organ studies would have to establish benefit, rejection risks, dangerous rhythms and the need for drugs that suppress immune rejection. This would define whether recipients can safely rely on the heart.

milestones.label: Reliable production and delivery work within defined clinical boundaries
milestones.explanation: Independent teams and manufacturing batches would have to deliver consistent organs, with validated preservation, transport, surgery and recipient eligibility. This would establish where replacement can reliably work.

uncertain: The pumping thresholds, manufacturing tolerances, comparison treatments and follow-up needed to judge success remain undefined.
It is unknown whether using a patient's own cells would reliably reduce rejection or the need for immune-suppressing drugs.
The production capacity, affordability and delivery systems needed for broad access remain unproven.

page.title: Tissue-engineered human hearts for transplantation
page.definition: A manufactured living human heart replaces the recipient’s native heart and sustains circulation. Its muscle, blood vessels, valves and electrical conduction system—the cells that coordinate each beat—function together as a whole organ.

goal.need: The United States added more new heart-transplant candidates than it performed heart transplants in 2024. A manufactured living replacement heart is pursued as a source of organs that does not require donation of a whole heart.

figures.caption: United States heart-transplant activity in 2024
figures.note: Candidates listed at multiple centres are counted once per listing. These annual counts concern different cohorts; their difference does not measure unmet need.

completion.title: The European Commission authorises an engineered human heart for whole-heart replacement.
completion.criterion: The European Commission grants centralised marketing authorisation to a tissue-engineered living human heart specifically for replacement of the native heart and support of the recipient’s circulation. The authorised indication, patient population, manufacturing specifications and concomitant treatments define the demonstrated scope.
completion.set_by: European Commission and European Medicines Agency, EU marketing-authorisation framework for tissue-engineered advanced therapy medicinal products.
completion.threshold_quote: The data on safety and efficacy will be carefully assessed by the competent authorities before a product receives marketing authorisation.
completion.basis: The EU framework covers tissue-engineered medicines and assesses quality, safety, efficacy and benefit–risk balance. Authorisation for the whole-organ indication supplies an external clinical completion test. The framework does not prescribe a universal survival duration or pumping threshold for an engineered replacement heart.

milestones.title: A bioprinted heart pumps 3–6 L/min in a perfusion model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate bioprinted-heart function in a perfusion model. PRINT lists heart rate 60–120 beats/min, cardiac output 3–6 L/min and ejection fraction 50–70% (the fraction of ventricular blood ejected per beat). These are programme benchmarks, with justified alternatives permitted, rather than a complete release specification. Min et al., published on 22 March 2024, demonstrated perfused cardiac-tissue culture and improved maturation, without demonstrating a replacement organ.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, PRINT Innovative Solutions Opening of 9 April 2024, Table 2, M3.5. The heart-specific numerical benchmarks appear in a table; section 1.3 permits justified alternative metrics.

milestones.title: Bioprinted hearts are implanted in more than 10 small animals and show 3–6-month graft survival.
milestones.criterion: Successfully implant bioprinted hearts in more than 10 small animals; demonstrate graft viability and longevity with 3–6-month survival, safety and immune compatibility without teratomas, rejection, toxicity or mutagenicity; and demonstrate normal organ structure and host response at postmortem examination. PRINT does not specify a required survivor fraction.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, PRINT Innovative Solutions Opening of 9 April 2024, Table 2, M3.6. These table-only targets concern bioprinted organs, including hearts, and allow justified alternative metrics.

milestones.title: Bioprinted hearts show 3–6-month graft survival and normal function in large animals.
milestones.criterion: Successfully implant bioprinted hearts in more than 5 large animals, demonstrate 3–6-month graft survival and normal heart function, and show no teratomas, rejection or toxicity at 6 months. PRINT lists heart rate 60–120 beats/min, cardiac output 3–6 L/min and ejection fraction 50–70%; no survivor fraction is specified. Jebran et al., published on 29 January 2025, studied muscle grafts on retained macaque hearts: 7 animals had 3-month follow-up and 13 had 6-month follow-up.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, PRINT Innovative Solutions Opening of 9 April 2024, Table 2, M3.10. The heart-function benchmarks appear in a table; justified alternative metrics are permitted.

milestones.title: A person receives an engineered whole heart in an authorised first-in-human clinical trial.
milestones.criterion: A person receives a tissue-engineered living human heart as whole-heart replacement in an authorised clinical trial: the product’s first administration to humans. This milestone establishes clinical use without assigning an unsupported survival duration. Jebran et al. examined retained graft muscle in one patient’s explanted native heart about 3 months after implantation; that intervention repaired a retained heart.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, EudraCT section E.7, published definition of Phase I and first administration to humans. This is a general clinical-development stage, not a whole-heart protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: It includes the first administration of that product in human subjects.

milestones.title: An engineered whole-heart replacement demonstrates clinical efficacy on meaningful endpoints.
milestones.criterion: Clinical studies of whole-heart replacement demonstrate efficacy using clinically meaningful endpoints, establish duration of effect and support benefit–risk assessment against existing treatments. EMA sets no universal sample size or follow-up duration. The report dated 28 May 2026 concerns BioVAT muscle grafts in 20 patients: 12 of 16 receiving the maximal dose completed 3-month interim follow-up; the adjusted mean ejection-fraction increase was 3.9 percentage points (90% CI 0.9–6.8). All 20 had adverse events and 3 died. This open-label repair study does not establish whole-heart replacement efficacy.
milestones.set_by: EMA Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, Guideline on human cell-based medicinal products, section 4.4.5. This general efficacy criterion covers tissue-engineered products; no whole-heart-specific clinical endpoint is supplied.
milestones.threshold_quote: Clinical efficacy studies should be adequate to demonstrate efficacy in the target patient population using clinically meaningful endpoints

milestones.title: EMA recommends authorisation of an engineered human heart for whole-heart replacement.
milestones.criterion: After assessment of the engineered heart’s quality, safety and efficacy by EMA’s Committee for Advanced Therapies, the Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use adopts a positive opinion recommending European Commission authorisation specifically for whole-heart replacement. This is the scientific recommendation preceding the Commission’s authorisation decision.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, published centralised assessment procedure for advanced therapy medicinal products.
milestones.threshold_quote: the CHMP adopts an opinion recommending or not the authorisation of the medicine by the European Commission.

not_found: No registered whole-heart replacement trial or human transplantation of a complete engineered heart was located in searches of PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA, EMA and PRINT.
No whole-heart-specific human survival threshold, numerical clinical efficacy endpoint or follow-up duration was located in the regulatory and programme documents searched.
The Jebran full text could not be reopened from Nature or PMC; the previously checked Atlas source supports the graft findings.
The NEJM BioVAT-HF full text was inaccessible; its indexed abstract supplied the interim clinical results.
A publication year for the Texas Heart Institute FAQ was not found.

results.finding: In 15 rats, engineered heart muscle was assessed 4 weeks after implantation.
results.detail: Seven rats received viable grafts and eight received irradiated grafts. The implants were muscle loops for heart repair, not bioprinted whole hearts, and follow-up was shorter than 3–6 months.
results.quote:
rhesus macaque CMs could be identified 4 weeks after implantation of 
viable but not lethally irradiated EHM

results.finding: Engineered heart muscle grafts in 13 macaques had 6-month follow-up.
results.detail: The grafts were muscle patches placed on retained hearts, not bioprinted whole hearts. Some grafts were rejected under particular immunosuppression conditions; functional improvement was observed in some animals.
results.quote:
here we report on tissue-engineered myocardial heart 
muscle allograft and autograft implantation with long-term follow-up 
(n = 7 for 3 months and n  = 13 for 6 months)

results.finding: One trial patient had engineered heart muscle grafts visible 3 months after implantation.
results.detail: The authorised trial implanted muscle grafts to repair the patient's retained heart. The patient subsequently received a conventional heart transplant; the engineered grafts were not a whole-heart replacement.
results.quote:
Explanted heart obtained

results.finding: Flow-cultured human cardiac tissues (n=20) beat at 76.59 ± 15.7 beats/min.
results.detail: The study cultured cardiac tissue in a perfused microfluidic chip. It did not demonstrate a bioprinted whole heart or measure its cardiac output or ejection fraction.

results.finding: Bioprinted chambered cardiac organoids (n = 7) had a mean ejection fraction of 0.7%.
results.detail: The small, valve-free organoids were perfusable and demonstrated pump dynamics, but their ejection fraction was below the programme benchmark. The study did not report a 3–6 L/min cardiac output; pump measurements were made in a culture-medium bath.
results.quote: Based on these values, we calculated an ejection fraction of 0.7% on average, with a maximum value of 6.5%
